new_statements.quote: As noted above in several examples, excessively long and/or high tone is associated with intensity. It has also been observed that in some languages (e.g. Grebo, Glaro), low tone seems more frequent in a general count of ideophones in the lexicon. However, such tonal correlations, semantic or of other sorts, are clearly an area for further research.
new_statements.citation: Zogbo, Lynell Marchese. 2022. Ideophones in the Kru language family. Language in Africa 3(1): 84-143. doi:10.37892/2686-8946-2022-3-1-84-143
new_statements.locator: sec. 3.3.5 'Tone patterns', printed p.107 (the text); Table 1 p.90; family note p.92 (the text)
new_statements.relation_note: Family-level: 'Kru languages have three or four contrastive tones and various modifications (Marchese 1979; 1989)' (p.92); Glaro-specific only incidentally: in Grebo and Glaro 'low tone seems more frequent in a general count of ideophones in the lexicon' (p.107), which presupposes lexical tone in Glaro; Glaro ideophones are cited in practical orthography with tone diacritics (gbòó, gbàóó, srǒǒǒ). Nothing on word stress (the words 'stress' on pp. 103, 105, 113 refer to expressive emphasis in ideophones generally, not to a Glaro stress system).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Glaro is treated as a Kru tone language (family: three or four contrastive level tones); the only Glaro-specific remark is that low tone predominates in its ideophone inventory; no tone count for Glaro and no stress statement.
new_statements.identity_note: Lesley Wolfe (New Tribes Mission, Béoué, Côte d'Ivoire) is the Western Glaro source already recorded for glar1241 (Zogbo 2019 fn., 'Wolfe p.c.'); Glaro-Twabo [glr]. [name in source: Glaro (Western Kru; data 'Lesley Wolfe and Bàrǐ Klé Eugene (p.c.)', Table 1); pages 90 (Table 1, sources), 92 (family phonology note), 93 (ex. 2 Glaro ideophones), 107 (tone remark naming Glaro), exx. 28, 68, 99, 101 passim]
